explanation: Memoize the best value obtainable from items 0 through k with a given remaining capacity. Compare skipping item k with taking it, if it fits, then recurse only on earlier items.
timeComplexity: O(n(C+1)) upper bound: n item stages and C+1 capacities, with two transitions per state. Every item-capacity state compares taking and skipping; descending one-row updates use O(C) rather than O(nC) storage.
spaceComplexity: O(n(C+1)) memo storage plus O(n) recursion. The one-row update keeps capacity+1 values; native recursion stores item/capacity states and its call chain.
attribution: Unmodified reference from epi_judge_python_solutions/knapsack.py; Elements of Programming Interviews Judge contributors; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 International, retained in repository LICENSE. Explanation authored for EPI Practice.
correctness: Every feasible subset either excludes item k or includes it once. Removing an included item leaves exactly the residual-capacity problem on earlier items. The maximum of these exhaustive alternatives is optimal, and reducing k in both branches prevents reuse.
walkthrough: For items (weight,value) [(2,7),(3,9),(4,12)] and capacity 5, choosing the first two gives weight 5 and value 16. The last item alone gives only 12, so the answer remains 16. JSON arguments are [items,capacity], with each item [weight,value]. C#/JavaScript use pair records and native wrappers construct Item records.
edgeCases: An item is selected at most once, including a zero-weight item.
Capacity zero permits zero-weight items but no positive-weight item.
Skipping all items allows value zero even when values are negative.
Item records are (weight,value), not the reverse.
